stimuli.title: Passage 1: Lights on the Edge of the Sea
stimuli.text:
**A** For most of the history of seafaring, the coast was more dangerous to a ship than the open ocean. Out at sea, a vessel had room to make mistakes; near land, a single error in judging position could put it on rocks within minutes. Sailors therefore learned to read the shore by day, picking out church towers, distinctive hills and the colour of cliffs. At night, however, these landmarks vanished, and for centuries the only help a captain could hope for was a fire burning on a headland. The most famous early light, the Pharos of Alexandria, was built in the third century BC, but it was an exception. Most early lights were simple open fires of wood or coal, often tended irregularly and easily confused with the hearths of nearby villages.

**B** The open fire had a deeper weakness than its unreliability: most of its light was wasted. A fire radiates in every direction, upwards into the sky and backwards over the land as much as out to sea. Even when coal braziers were placed high on stone towers, a ship a few miles offshore might see no more than a dull glow. In stormy weather, when a light was needed most, rain and spray could reduce it to almost nothing. Enclosing the flame in a glazed lantern protected it from wind and rain, but the glass quickly blackened with soot, and keepers spent long nights cleaning panes that were dirty again within the hour.

**C** The first real improvement came in the late eighteenth century with the lamp designed by the Swiss physicist Aimé Argand. His burner used a hollow, circular wick and a glass chimney that drew a steady current of air through the centre of the flame. The result was a light far brighter than a candle and almost free of smoke. Lighthouse engineers combined the new lamp with polished metal reflectors shaped like shallow bowls, which gathered the light that would otherwise have escaped and sent it out in a concentrated beam. A single tower might now carry a dozen or more lamps, each with its own reflector, arranged in rows facing the sea.

**D** Reflectors had their own limitations. The silvered surfaces tarnished and had to be polished daily, and even a well-kept mirror lost a large share of the light falling on it. The solution came from the French engineer Augustin-Jean Fresnel, who in the 1820s proposed replacing a single heavy lens with a series of concentric glass rings, each shaped to bend light towards the horizon. Because each ring was thin, the lens was far lighter than a solid one of the same power, and it absorbed much less light. A lamp at the centre of a large Fresnel lens could be seen from distances that earlier lights could not approach, and within a few decades such lenses had been fitted to lighthouses on many of the world's busiest coasts.

**E** Brightness alone, however, did not solve the navigator's problem. On a coast with several lighthouses, a captain who saw a light still had to know which one it was. Engineers responded by giving each light its own character. Some shone steadily, some flashed at fixed intervals, and others were hidden at regular moments by rotating screens. The pattern of a particular light, such as two flashes every ten seconds, was printed in published lists and on charts, so that a sailor with a watch could identify a tower simply by timing it. The lists were updated as new towers were built or old ones changed, and an out-of-date list could be almost as dangerous as no list at all. Colour was also used, although red and green glass absorbed so much light that coloured lights had a much shorter range than white ones.

**F** During the twentieth century the role of the keeper slowly disappeared. Electric lamps replaced oil, clockwork rotation gave way to electric motors, and remote monitoring meant that a fault could be reported to a central station without anyone on site. In Britain the last staffed lighthouses were automated in the 1990s. Today satellite positioning has made many lights less essential than they once were, and some authorities have reduced the range of their lights or switched them off altogether. Yet many remain in service, partly because electronic systems can fail and partly because a light seen from the deck offers a kind of reassurance that no screen can provide.

stimuli.title: Passage 2: Frozen Archives
stimuli.text:
**A** In a laboratory on the edge of a university campus, a technician slides open a drawer and lifts out a foil packet no bigger than an envelope. Inside are several thousand seeds of a wild grass that grows on only a few hillsides. If those hillsides were ploughed or burned tomorrow, the packet would hold the species' best chance of survival. Collections like this one, known as seed banks, now exist in many countries, and together they store millions of samples of crops and wild plants. The work is unglamorous: much of it involves counting, labelling and checking, and the freezers must be watched day and night in case of a fault.

**B** The idea is older than it might seem. Plant collectors have exchanged and stored seeds for centuries, but early collections were kept at room temperature and had to be grown out and harvested again every few years to stay alive. This was slow and costly, and every replanting risked losing rare varieties to disease, cross-pollination or simple human error. The modern seed bank emerged in the twentieth century, when researchers showed that many seeds could survive for decades if they were first dried and then kept cold.

**C** The process begins with drying. Freshly collected seeds may hold a large share of their weight in water, and in that state they would be damaged by ice crystals when frozen. In a drying room kept at low humidity, the moisture is gradually drawn out over several weeks until it falls to only a few per cent. The seeds are then cleaned, counted, sealed in airtight packets and placed in freezers, typically at around minus eighteen degrees Celsius. Each packet is labelled with the place and date of collection, so that later researchers know exactly where the plants came from. Under these conditions, the seeds of many species are expected to remain alive for a century or longer.

**D** Storage is not the end of the work. No one can tell simply by looking whether a seed is still alive, so samples are tested at intervals. A small number of seeds are taken from a packet and placed on damp paper in warm, bright conditions; the proportion that germinate gives an estimate of the health of the whole sample. When this figure falls below a set level, the collection must be renewed by growing plants from the remaining seeds and gathering a fresh harvest. Because each test uses up seeds, banks try to store enough for decades of checking.

**E** Not every plant cooperates. The seeds of some species, including many tropical trees, are killed by drying, and they cannot be stored by the usual method. Botanists call these seeds recalcitrant. For them, researchers have turned to cryopreservation: tiny pieces of tissue, often the embryo removed from the seed, are cooled rapidly in liquid nitrogen to nearly minus two hundred degrees. The technique is demanding, and each species may require months of trials to find a method that works, but it offers the only long-term option for plants that would otherwise survive only in the wild. As a result, seed banks hold far fewer samples of these plants than of crops such as wheat and rice, whose seeds dry and store easily.

**F** The best-known collection is the Svalbard Global Seed Vault, cut into a mountainside on a Norwegian island far inside the Arctic Circle and opened in 2008. It holds duplicate samples deposited by banks around the world, a back-up in case the originals are lost to war, natural disaster or equipment failure. Each depositing bank keeps ownership of its own samples, which can be withdrawn only by the bank that sent them. Its location was chosen partly because the surrounding permafrost would keep the samples cold even if the power failed. Supporters stress, however, that the vault is a last resort. Seeds in storage cannot adapt to a changing climate, and many scientists believe that protecting plants in their natural habitats must remain the first line of defence.

stimuli.title: Passage 3: In Praise of Boredom
stimuli.text:
Few states of mind have as poor a reputation as boredom. Parents treat it as a problem to be fixed, employers as a sign of disengagement, and the technology industry as an empty space waiting to be filled. Smartphones in particular have made it possible never to be bored again: any pause, whether in a queue, on a train or in the minutes before sleep, can now be occupied instantly. It is worth asking, however, whether we have been too quick to treat boredom as an enemy. A growing body of research suggests that it may serve a purpose, and that losing it entirely could cost us more than we realise.

The case begins with what boredom actually is. The psychologist Hannah Merrow describes it not as a lack of stimulation but as a signal: an unpleasant feeling that tells us our current activity is failing to engage us and that we should look for something else. In this view boredom works rather like hunger. Nobody enjoys being hungry, but a person who never felt hunger would be in serious danger. A person who never feels bored, Merrow argues, may lose the push that drives them to seek new goals.

Some of the most widely reported studies have examined boredom and creativity. In one experiment conducted by Daniel Ostrowski and colleagues, volunteers first spent fifteen minutes copying numbers from a long printed list, a task chosen precisely because it was dull. They were then asked to think of as many uses as possible for a pair of plastic cups. Compared with a group who had not done the copying, the bored volunteers produced more ideas, and their ideas were judged more original. Ostrowski is careful not to claim too much. The effect, he notes, was modest, and it has not appeared in every attempt to repeat the study. Nevertheless, the findings fit a wider pattern: when the mind is not occupied by a task, it tends to wander, and mind-wandering appears to help people make unexpected connections.

I find this research persuasive, but I think its enthusiasts sometimes overstate their case. Boredom is not a magic source of inspiration, and for some people it is genuinely harmful. The sociologist Priya Anand has shown that chronic boredom, the kind experienced over months or years in unrewarding work or enforced idleness, is linked to poorer mental health and to risky behaviour. There is a difference between the brief boredom of a long train journey and the grinding boredom of a life with too few opportunities. Praising the first should never become an excuse for ignoring the second.

What, then, is the problem with filling every quiet moment? The difficulty lies in how we respond to the signal. Merrow points out that boredom presents a choice: we can look for a meaningful new activity, or we can reach for the quickest available distraction. The phone almost always wins, because it offers relief in seconds and asks nothing of us in return. The feeling disappears, but so does the push towards anything better. Over time, Anand suggests, people may become less tolerant of even short pauses, so that a few minutes without input begins to feel unbearable.

Children are often at the centre of this debate. Many parents feel guilty when a child complains of having nothing to do, and they respond by arranging activities or handing over a screen. Teachers I have spoken to describe pupils who struggle to stay with a problem for more than a few minutes before asking for help. It would be wrong to blame screens alone for this, since crowded timetables and pressure to achieve also leave little room for unstructured time. But I believe that children who are occasionally left to be bored, and to find their own way out of it, learn something valuable about their own resources.

None of this means that we should seek out boredom for its own sake, or that the dull meeting and the delayed train are secretly good for us. The point is narrower. Boredom is uncomfortable because it is meant to be, and its discomfort can lead somewhere useful if we allow it to. Rather than banishing it with a swipe, we might occasionally let it run its course, and see where the wandering mind takes us. The result will not always be a brilliant idea. Sometimes it will simply be the realisation that we would rather be doing something else, which is, after all, exactly what boredom was trying to tell us.

stimuli.title: Passage 1: Messages Through the Pipes
stimuli.text:
**A** In the second half of the nineteenth century, the telegraph could carry a message across a continent in minutes, yet the same message might take hours to cross the city at the other end. Telegraph offices were usually located in business districts, and the final stage of every journey depended on messenger boys on foot or on horse-drawn carts struggling through crowded streets. Businesses complained that a telegram from another country could reach the city faster than it could be carried the last mile to their door. As trade grew, so did the delay, and city authorities began to look for a faster way to move paper between buildings.

**B** The answer they found was the pneumatic tube. The principle was simple: a cylinder, or carrier, containing documents is placed inside a sealed pipe, and air pressure behind it, or a partial vacuum in front of it, pushes it along. Engineers had experimented with the idea earlier in the century, but it became practical only when steam-driven pumps could produce a strong and steady flow of air. The pipes themselves were usually made of iron and laid in trenches beneath the pavement, joining stations that were often only a few kilometres apart. London, Berlin and Paris all built networks in the 1860s, and by the end of the century many other cities had followed.

**C** A typical message passed through several stages. A clerk first rolled the paper and placed it in a leather or metal carrier, which was then loaded into the tube at a sending station. Pumps at a central engine house drove the carrier to a sorting office, where staff removed it, read the address and sent it on along a second line towards the station nearest its destination. From there a messenger completed the last short distance on foot. In Paris, where the system grew into one of the largest in the world, a letter sent this way could cross the city in an hour or two. Messages sent by tube were usually short notes rather than long letters, since a carrier held only a few sheets, and they cost more to send than ordinary post.

**D** The tubes were not only a tool for the post office. Department stores used them to carry cash and receipts between sales counters and a central cash office, so that shop assistants never had to keep large sums of money at their tills. Stock exchanges relied on them to move orders between the trading floor and brokers' offices, and hospitals later adopted them to send samples to laboratories. Large libraries used similar systems to send requests for books from reading rooms to the stacks. In many of these buildings the tubes survived long after the city networks had closed.

**E** Expansion brought difficulties. The tubes ran beneath streets that were constantly being dug up for gas, water and later electricity, and every repair risked damaging a pipe. Carriers sometimes jammed, and finding the blockage could mean opening the road at several points. In very cold weather, moisture inside the pipes could freeze and slow the carriers down. Running the pumps was expensive, and as traffic grew the networks needed more stations and more staff. Supporters argued that these costs were justified by speed, but by the early twentieth century a cheaper rival was spreading rapidly: the telephone.

**F** The decline was gradual rather than sudden. Many systems were closed in the middle of the century, though some lasted much longer: the Paris network carried messages until 1984, and the system in Prague was still operating when floods damaged it in 2002. Today the tubes are often remembered as a curiosity, yet the basic idea has not disappeared. In some cities, sections of old tube still lie beneath the streets, long after the last carrier passed through them. Engineers proposing high-speed transport in low-pressure tubes have described their plans as heirs to the pneumatic post, though whether such schemes will ever carry passengers remains uncertain.

stimuli.title: Passage 2: Guardians of the Coast
stimuli.text:
**A** Along tropical and subtropical coastlines, where rivers meet the sea and the tide floods and drains twice a day, grow forests unlike any others. Mangroves are trees and shrubs that have adapted to life in salty, waterlogged mud that would kill most plants within days. They are found on the shores of more than a hundred countries, from the deltas of South Asia to the lagoons of West Africa and the Caribbean, yet for much of the twentieth century they were regarded as little more than wasteland: smelly, full of mosquitoes and in the way of development. In some places the forests form a narrow fringe along the shore; in others, especially in large river deltas, they cover wide areas of land that is flooded at high tide.

**B** Their survival depends on a set of remarkable adaptations. Some species filter out most of the salt as water enters their roots; others absorb it and then excrete it through special glands on their leaves, which may be seen glittering with crystals. Because the mud contains almost no oxygen, many mangroves send up pencil-like roots that stick out of the ground and take in air at low tide, while others are supported by arching prop roots that hold the trunk above the water like the legs of a stool. Several species even produce seedlings that begin growing while still attached to the parent tree, then drop into the water and float until they lodge in suitable mud.

**C** It is the tangle of roots that makes mangroves so valuable to people living behind them. When waves enter a mangrove forest, they lose energy as they pass between the trunks and roots, and their height falls with every metre travelled. The roots also trap mud carried in by the tide, and in some places this slowly raises the level of the land behind the forest. Field measurements suggest that a wide belt of mature forest can greatly reduce the height of ordinary storm waves before they reach the shore. Mangroves are not a complete defence: a very large storm surge can still sweep through them. But villages sheltered by healthy forest have often suffered less damage than neighbouring settlements on cleared coasts. For this reason, some engineers now recommend keeping or replanting mangroves in front of sea walls, so that the forest takes the first force of the waves.

**D** The forests also help to slow climate change. Mangrove soils are waterlogged and low in oxygen, so dead leaves and roots decay very slowly and their carbon builds up in the mud over centuries. Scientists who study this "blue carbon" have found that, area for area, mangrove soils can hold far more carbon than many forests on dry land. When mangroves are cleared and the mud is dug out or left to dry, much of that stored carbon may be released into the atmosphere.

**E** Despite these benefits, large areas of mangrove have been lost in recent decades. The forests have been cleared for coastal building, for rice fields and especially for ponds used to farm shrimp, many of which are abandoned after a few years when disease or pollution makes them unproductive. Cutting for timber and charcoal has thinned others. Coastal roads and sea walls can also cut mangroves off from the tides they need. Because the trees grow in a narrow strip between land and sea, even modest clearing can break a forest into fragments that no longer protect the shore.

**F** Many governments and charities now plant mangroves, but early efforts taught hard lessons. In some projects, seedlings were planted on open mudflats that looked empty but lay too low and were covered by the tide for too long each day; almost all of them died. Ecologists now argue that the most successful restoration begins not with planting but with restoring the flow of water, for example by breaking through old pond walls, so that seeds carried by the tide can settle naturally where conditions suit them. Planting may still help, but only where mangroves grew before. Local communities are often closely involved in this work, since they are usually the first to notice when an area begins to recover.

stimuli.title: Passage 3: Do Museums Still Need Objects?
stimuli.text:
When a museum announces that it has created a precise digital copy of one of its treasures, the news is usually greeted with enthusiasm. High-resolution scanning can now record the surface of a sculpture to a fraction of a millimetre, and a visitor on the other side of the world can rotate it on a screen, zoom in on a chisel mark and read the curator's notes, all without buying a ticket. Some commentators have gone further and asked whether museums need to keep and display so many original objects at all. I want to argue that this question, though worth asking, rests on a misunderstanding of what museums are for.

The case for the digital museum is not foolish, and it deserves a fair hearing. The design writer Lena Fogarty points out that most large museums display only a small fraction of their collections; the rest is kept in storage, where it is seen by almost no one. Digitising these hidden objects, she argues, would make them available to students and researchers who could never travel to see them. The historian Marcus Webb adds a further argument: many objects in Western museums were taken from other countries in circumstances that are now widely questioned, and high-quality copies could allow originals to be returned while the museum continues to tell their story. Both points seem to me entirely reasonable, and neither requires us to abandon the original object.

Where the argument goes wrong is in assuming that a copy can do everything the original does. Some of what an object communicates can certainly be captured digitally: its shape, its colour and its decoration. But visitors consistently report that standing in front of a real object is a different experience from looking at an image of it. The museum educator Ruth Okafor, who has interviewed hundreds of visitors, finds that people describe a sense of connection with the past that they do not feel when looking at reproductions, even very good ones. She is cautious about explaining this feeling, but she notes that it is strongest when visitors know that the object in front of them was handled by the people who made and used it.

Sceptics may reply that this is mere sentiment, a kind of superstition about authenticity. Perhaps it is. But sentiment is not a trivial matter in an institution whose purpose is to help people care about the past. A museum that offered only copies might inform, but I doubt that it would move its visitors in the same way, and a public that is not moved is unlikely to support the expensive work of conservation and research on which our knowledge of the past depends. Museums have always depended on the public to value what they hold, whether through ticket sales, donations or the taxes that pay for national collections.

There is also a scholarly reason for keeping originals. Every copy records only what its makers thought to record. A scan made today captures the surface of an object, but it tells us nothing about the chemistry of its paint or the source of its metal, and it cannot answer questions that no one has yet thought to ask. No museum can predict which of those questions will matter in fifty years. Again and again, new techniques have drawn information from objects that were assumed to have given up all their secrets decades earlier. Webb himself accepts this point, and he does not suggest that originals should be destroyed, only that they need not always be on display.

None of this is an argument against digitisation. On the contrary, I believe every museum should be scanning its collections as fast as funding allows. Copies can widen access, support research and preserve knowledge if an original is damaged. A good digital model can also let visitors examine the underside of a statue or the inside of a vessel, views that no gallery could safely offer. The mistake is to see copies and originals as competitors, when they are better understood as partners. The best digital collections send people to see the real thing, and the best galleries use digital tools to explain what visitors are looking at.

The real threat to museums is not the scanner but the budget. Conservation is slow and expensive, and when funds are short it is tempting to believe that a digital record can stand in for the care of the object itself. It cannot. Digital files need care too: formats become obsolete, and storage must be paid for year after year. If we allow copies to become an excuse for neglecting originals, we may one day find that the copy is all we have left.

stimuli.title: The Box That Changed Trade
stimuli.text:
**A** Before the middle of the twentieth century, loading a cargo ship was slow and costly work. Goods arrived at the docks in sacks, barrels, crates and bales of every size, and teams of dockworkers carried or hoisted each item into the hold, where it had to be packed by hand so that it would not shift at sea. A large ship could spend a week or more in port being loaded and unloaded, and theft and damage were common.

**B** The idea of packing goods into standard boxes had been tried before, but it is usually credited to Malcom McLean, an American trucking businessman. In 1956 a converted tanker, the Ideal X, sailed from Newark to Houston carrying fifty-eight metal containers that could be lifted directly from lorries onto the deck. McLean's insight was not the box itself but the system around it: ships, cranes, lorries and trains designed so that a container could move between them without ever being opened.

**C** At first, different companies used boxes of different sizes, which meant that a container from one line might not fit another's ships or cranes. During the 1960s, international standards were agreed for the dimensions of containers and for the corner fittings by which they are lifted and locked together. The twenty-foot box became the industry's unit of measurement, so that a ship's capacity is still described in twenty-foot equivalent units.

**D** The effects on ports were dramatic. Cranes could now move a container in minutes, and a ship that once spent a week in harbour could be turned around far more quickly. Fewer dockworkers were needed, and in many old port cities the busy waterfront districts declined as shipping moved to new terminals with deep water and large areas of flat land for stacking boxes.

**E** Cheaper shipping also changed what was made where. When the cost of moving goods across an ocean became a small share of their price, manufacturers could build factories far from their customers and assemble products from parts made in several countries. Some economists argue that the container did more to expand world trade than many trade agreements.

**F** The system has weaknesses. Because so much depends on a few very large ports and shipping routes, a blockage in one place can delay goods around the world. Containers also make it harder for customs officers to check what is inside, since only a small proportion can be opened and searched.

stimuli.title: How Birds Find Their Way
stimuli.text:
**A** Each autumn, billions of birds leave their breeding grounds and fly to the places where they will spend the winter, some covering thousands of kilometres. Many young birds make this journey alone on their first attempt, without parents to follow, and yet they arrive in roughly the right place. How they manage it has puzzled naturalists for centuries, and the answer, it now seems, is that birds use not one method but several.

**B** The sun is one guide. In experiments carried out in the 1950s, caged starlings became restless at migration time and tended to face in their normal direction of travel. When mirrors were used to shift the apparent position of the sun, the birds shifted their direction to match. Because the sun moves across the sky during the day, a bird using it as a compass must also keep track of the time, which it appears to do with an internal body clock.

**C** Many songbirds migrate at night, and for them the stars matter. Researchers raising young birds under the artificial sky of a planetarium found that the birds learned to orient themselves by the part of the sky around which the stars appear to turn. When the projected sky was made to rotate around a different star, the birds adjusted accordingly, which suggested that they were learning the pattern rather than being born with a fixed map.

**D** Birds can also sense the Earth's magnetic field. In tests using artificial magnetic fields, birds changed the direction they faced when the field around them was altered. How they detect the field is still debated. One theory points to chemical reactions in the eye that may be affected by magnetism, which would mean that birds could in some sense see the field; another focuses on tiny particles of iron-containing material in the beak.

**E** Some seabirds seem to rely on smell. Shearwaters whose sense of smell had been temporarily blocked were able to fly normally but had great difficulty finding their way home across open sea, while birds whose magnetic sense had been disturbed did much better. Over featureless water, odours carried by the wind may provide a kind of map that the other senses cannot.

**F** No single cue explains everything, and birds appear to check one against another. Clouds can hide the sun and stars, and magnetic readings vary from place to place, so a system with several back-ups is more reliable than any one sense alone. Young birds may also make mistakes that older birds avoid: experienced travellers that are blown off course are often better at returning to their usual route than first-year birds.

stimuli.title: What Happens Inside a Loaf
stimuli.text:
**A** Bread is one of the oldest prepared foods, and for most of its history it was made without any understanding of the chemistry involved. Bakers knew that dough left in a warm place would rise, and that a piece kept back from one batch could start the next, but they had no idea why. Today food scientists can describe each stage of bread making in detail, and their explanations show how much happens inside an ordinary loaf.

**B** The structure of bread begins with gluten. Wheat flour contains two groups of proteins which, when mixed with water and worked by kneading, link together into long, stretchy chains. These form a network that runs through the dough, giving it the elastic quality that bakers feel under their hands. Flours with little of these proteins, such as those from rice or maize, cannot form the same network, which is why they give flat or crumbly results when used on their own.

**C** The rise itself comes from yeast, a single-celled fungus that feeds on sugars in the dough. As it feeds, it releases carbon dioxide gas and small amounts of alcohol. The gas is trapped by the gluten network in countless tiny bubbles, which expand and cause the dough to swell. Warmth speeds this process up, but dough that rises too quickly may develop less flavour, and many bakers prefer a long, cool rise.

**D** Sourdough works in a similar way but relies on a mixture of wild yeasts and bacteria kept alive in a starter of flour and water. The bacteria produce acids that give the bread its sharp taste and help it stay fresh for longer. Because the starter is fed and kept from one batch to the next, some bakeries claim that theirs has been in continuous use for decades.

**E** In the oven, several changes happen at once. The gas bubbles expand rapidly in the heat, giving the loaf a final burst of growth, until the proteins set and the structure becomes fixed. On the surface, where the temperature rises highest, sugars and proteins react together to form the brown crust and many of the flavours that people associate with fresh bread.

**F** Once baked, bread begins to go stale. Many people assume this is because it dries out, but the main cause is a change in the starch, which slowly returns to a more ordered, crystal-like form that feels hard and dry. This process happens fastest at temperatures just above freezing, so bread kept in a refrigerator usually goes stale sooner than bread kept at room temperature, while freezing almost stops it.

stimuli.title: The Four-Day Week: A Change Worth Making?
stimuli.text:
For most of the past century, the five-day working week has seemed as natural as the seasons. Yet it is a relatively recent invention, and there is nothing fixed about it. Over the last decade, a growing number of employers have experimented with a four-day week, usually keeping pay the same while reducing hours. The results have attracted a great deal of attention, and I believe they deserve it, although not all of the claims made for the idea stand up to scrutiny.

The strongest evidence concerns well-being. The organisational psychologist Clara Henning, who has followed staff at several firms before and after the change, reports large falls in stress and in the number of days taken off sick. Employees told her that the extra day gave them time for exercise, family and the errands that otherwise crowded their weekends. These findings are consistent across very different workplaces, and I see little reason to doubt them.

Claims about productivity are another matter. Supporters often say that workers produce as much in four days as they once did in five, because they waste less time and concentrate harder. In some offices this appears to be true. But the economist Owen Pryce warns that many trials have been short, and that the organisations taking part chose to do so, which may mean they were already well suited to the change. Firms that struggled might simply not have volunteered. Until we have evidence from a wider range of employers over several years, it would be unwise to assume that output will always hold steady.

There is also the question of who benefits. A shorter week is easier to arrange in an office, where work can often be rescheduled, than in a hospital, a care home or a factory that must run continuously. Pryce points out that in such settings a four-day week for each worker usually means hiring more staff, which raises costs. The union researcher Amira Saleh adds that workers on low pay may prefer extra paid hours to an extra day off. If the policy spreads only among well-paid office workers, it could widen the gap between those jobs and the rest.

None of this persuades me that the idea should be dropped. The five-day week was itself once a radical demand, and it was adopted gradually, industry by industry, as employers found ways to make it work. Something similar may happen now. What we need is patience and careful measurement rather than either enthusiasm or alarm.

stimuli.title: The Myth of the Lone Genius
stimuli.text:
Popular history loves a lone genius. We are told that a single brilliant mind, working in isolation, suddenly sees what no one else has seen, and that the world is changed as a result. The story is attractive because it is simple and because it flatters the idea that greatness lies within individuals. But I think it is, in most cases, misleading, and that believing it has real costs.

Consider how inventions actually emerge. The historian of technology Felix Brandt has collected hundreds of cases in which two or more people arrived at the same discovery independently, often within months of each other. Such cases, he argues, show that ideas tend to appear when the knowledge and tools needed for them have become widely available, so that if one inventor had not made a breakthrough, another would probably have done so soon afterwards. I find his evidence difficult to dismiss.

The lone-genius story also hides the many people whose work made an achievement possible. Famous laboratories of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries were busy workplaces in which teams of assistants built equipment, ran tests and recorded results, yet their names rarely appear in popular accounts. The sociologist Ines Varela has studied the notebooks kept in such workplaces and finds that credit was often given to the person in charge for ideas that first appeared in the notes of junior staff.

None of this means that individuals do not matter. Some people clearly possess unusual talent, energy or imagination, and the psychologist Tom Adair has shown that outstanding creators tend to produce a very large amount of work, much of it unremarkable, from which their best ideas emerge. In other words, what looks like a sudden flash of genius is often the visible tip of years of effort. That, to my mind, is a more encouraging message than the myth, because it suggests that persistence counts for more than a mysterious gift.

Why does the myth matter? Partly because it shapes how we reward people. If we believe that progress depends on a few exceptional individuals, we may pour resources into them while neglecting the teams, institutions and shared knowledge that support their work. It may also discourage young people who do not see themselves as geniuses from attempting creative work at all. A more accurate story, in which discovery is collective and gradual, would be fairer and, I suspect, more productive.

stimuli.title: Is It Ever Too Late to Learn a Language?
stimuli.text:
It is widely believed that adults cannot learn a new language as well as children, and that anyone who starts after their teenage years is bound to struggle. Like many popular beliefs, this one contains some truth, but it has been stretched far beyond what the evidence supports, and I think it discourages many adults from trying.

The truth in the belief concerns pronunciation. Studies of immigrants who arrived in a new country at different ages consistently find that those who arrived as young children are far more likely to end up sounding like native speakers. The linguist Rosa Lindqvist, who has tested several thousand learners, finds that a native-like accent is rare among people who began after their early teens, though not impossible. On this point the evidence is strong, and I accept it.

Grammar and vocabulary are a different story. In the early stages of learning, adults often make faster progress than children, because they can understand explanations, use memory strategies and draw on knowledge of their first language. Children appear to catch up and overtake adults only after many years of living immersed in the language, an advantage that most adult learners, who study a few hours a week, never have the chance to test. Lindqvist's colleague Ahmed Karim argues that comparing a child surrounded by a language all day with an adult attending an evening class tells us more about opportunity than about age.

Motivation also matters, and here adults can have an advantage. An adult who needs a language for work, or to talk with a partner's family, may have reasons for persisting that a child in a school classroom lacks. The educational researcher Mei Tanaka has found that adults who set specific, practical goals, such as being able to follow a news broadcast, are more likely to keep studying than those whose aim is simply to become fluent.

I do not want to pretend that age makes no difference. An adult who starts learning at forty should not expect to pass as a native speaker, and should not feel that they have failed if they do not. But fluency in the sense that matters most, the ability to communicate with confidence and accuracy, is well within reach of most adults who are willing to put in the time. The belief that it is too late is, in the end, the greatest obstacle of all.

stimuli.title: Listening to the Reef
stimuli.text:
**A** Coral reefs are often described as among the most colourful places on Earth, but to a marine biologist with an underwater microphone they are also among the noisiest. A healthy reef crackles with the snapping of shrimp, the grunts and pops of fish and the scraping of animals feeding on coral. For a long time this noise was treated as little more than background, something to be filtered out of recordings. Over the past two decades, however, researchers have come to see it as a valuable source of information.

**B** Sound travels well underwater, much further than light, and young fish appear to use it to find a home. Many reef fish spend the first weeks of life drifting in open water as tiny larvae before returning to settle on a reef. Experiments in which recordings of reef noise were played through loudspeakers in open water found that larvae were attracted towards the sound, suggesting that noise acts as a kind of signpost leading them back to the reef.

**C** A damaged reef sounds very different. When corals die, as they may after a period of unusually warm water, the fish and other animals that depend on them often leave or die too, and the reef falls quiet. Recordings made on the same reefs before and after such events show the change clearly: a rich mixture of sounds gives way to a thinner, quieter one. Some scientists now suggest that sound recordings could be used to monitor the health of reefs cheaply, since a microphone left on the sea floor can record for weeks without a diver.

**D** This raised an intriguing question. If young fish are drawn to the sound of healthy reefs, and damaged reefs are quiet, could playing healthy sounds on a damaged reef help it recover? In one study on a damaged section of reef, researchers built small patches of dead coral and placed loudspeakers on some of them. Over several weeks, the patches with loudspeakers attracted considerably more young fish, and a wider range of species, than those left silent.

**E** The researchers are careful about what their results mean. Attracting fish is not the same as restoring a reef: if the water stays too warm or polluted, the corals will not recover and the fish may not survive. Loudspeakers are also expensive to maintain at sea. The scientists describe sound as one tool that might be combined with others, such as replanting coral fragments, rather than a cure on its own.

**F** Human noise adds another complication. The engines of ships and boats are loud underwater, and studies suggest that they can interfere with the ability of fish to hear each other and to detect predators. In busy coastal waters, the sounds of a healthy reef may be partly drowned out. Protecting the soundscape of the sea, some researchers argue, should become part of protecting the reefs themselves.

stimuli.title: From Weather Lore to Forecasts
stimuli.text:
For most of history, predicting the weather was a matter of proverbs and personal experience. Sailors and farmers watched the sky, the wind and the behaviour of animals, and some of their sayings contained real wisdom. But there was no way of knowing what weather was approaching from beyond the horizon, because no message could travel faster than the weather itself.

One of the first steps towards a scientific approach was a matter of language. In 1805 the British naval officer Francis Beaufort devised a scale for describing the strength of the wind, at first by its effect on the sails of a warship. A shared scale allowed observations made by different people at different times to be compared, which was essential if they were ever to be combined.

The electric telegraph, spreading in the mid-nineteenth century, changed everything, because reports of weather could now be sent across a country in minutes. Robert FitzRoy, who had commanded the survey ship on which Charles Darwin sailed, was appointed to head a new government department collecting weather information for use at sea. He set up a network of coastal stations that telegraphed their observations to London, and from these he issued warnings of storms to ports. In 1861 he began publishing what he called forecasts in a national newspaper. His predictions were often wrong, and he was ridiculed for them, but the storm warnings were valued by many sailors, and after they were stopped following his death in 1865, complaints from shipping interests soon brought them back.

Observation alone, however, could not explain why weather behaved as it did. In the early twentieth century, a group of scientists in the Norwegian city of Bergen, led by Vilhelm Bjerknes, developed the idea that the atmosphere contains large bodies of air with different temperatures, and that the boundaries between them, which they called fronts, are where much of the most changeable weather occurs. The term was chosen partly because the period was marked by the battlefronts of the First World War.

Bjerknes also believed that weather could in principle be calculated from the laws of physics. The English mathematician Lewis Fry Richardson attempted to do exactly that. Working largely by hand, he spent around six weeks calculating how the weather would change over a period of just six hours. His result was badly wrong, partly because of errors in the starting data, but his method was sound. He imagined a vast hall in which thousands of people would perform calculations together, fast enough to keep ahead of the real weather.

Richardson's dream came true in a form he could not have foreseen. When electronic computers appeared after the Second World War, they were soon applied to weather prediction, and methods descended from those he had worked out by hand became the basis of modern forecasting.

stimuli.title: Fresh Water from the Sea
stimuli.text:
**A** Less than three per cent of the world's water is fresh, and much of that is locked in ice or deep underground. For countries with dry climates and long coastlines, the sea is an obvious alternative source, and desalination, the removal of salt from seawater, now supplies drinking water to millions of people. The process is far from new, but the methods used have changed greatly.

**B** The oldest method is distillation. Seawater is heated until it turns to vapour, leaving the salt behind, and the vapour is then cooled so that it condenses as fresh water. Sailors used simple versions of this on board ship centuries ago. Large distillation plants are still found in some oil-producing regions, where cheap energy is available, but heating huge volumes of water uses a great deal of fuel.

**C** Most new plants use reverse osmosis instead. In this process, seawater is pushed at high pressure against a membrane, a thin sheet with pores so small that water molecules can pass through but most dissolved salts cannot. The fresh water collects on one side, and a concentrated salty liquid, known as brine, is left on the other. Because no heating is needed, reverse osmosis generally uses much less energy than distillation, although the pumps that create the pressure still require a large and steady supply of electricity.

**D** The membranes are delicate and easily blocked. Before seawater reaches them it must pass through a series of filters that remove sand, seaweed and tiny organisms. After treatment, the fresh water is so pure that it lacks the minerals found in natural drinking water, so small amounts of minerals are usually added back before it enters the supply, both for taste and to protect pipes from corrosion.

**E** The brine creates a further problem. For every litre of fresh water produced, a plant may discharge more than a litre of brine back into the sea. Because brine is heavier than seawater, it can sink and spread along the seabed, where it may harm plants and animals if it is not mixed well. Engineers now design outlets that spread the brine through many small openings so that it mixes quickly with the surrounding water. Some researchers are also exploring ways to extract useful materials from brine, turning a waste product into a resource.

stimuli.title: Before Banknotes
stimuli.text:
**A** Today most people think of money as notes, coins and numbers on a screen, but for much of history the idea that a piece of paper could be worth something would have seemed strange. Early forms of money were valuable in themselves: grain, cattle, shells and, above all, metals such as silver and gold. A coin was trusted because the metal it contained had value, whoever had made it.

**B** The first paper money appeared in China. During the Song dynasty, in the province of Sichuan, merchants used heavy iron coins, which were so awkward to carry in large amounts that traders began leaving them with trusted dealers in exchange for written receipts. These receipts could be passed from person to person, and in the early eleventh century the government took over their issue, creating what is generally regarded as the world's first official paper currency.

**C** Paper money offered clear advantages. It was light, easy to transport and cheap to produce compared with coins. But it also carried a new risk. Because the notes had no value in themselves, people accepted them only as long as they trusted the government that issued them. When rulers printed more notes to pay for wars or other expenses, the value of each note fell and prices rose.

**D** European travellers who reached China were astonished by the system. Marco Polo, who visited the court of the Mongol emperor in the late thirteenth century, described how paper made from the bark of mulberry trees was cut into notes, stamped with the emperor's seal and accepted throughout the empire. Many of his readers in Europe found the account hard to believe.

**E** Europe was slow to follow. Banks in several cities issued receipts for deposits of coin, but the first banknotes issued by a European bank are usually dated to 1661, when a bank in Stockholm began printing them. The experiment ended badly: too many notes were issued and the bank failed within a few years. Even so, the idea spread, and by the eighteenth century banknotes were in use across much of Europe.

**F** For centuries, many governments promised that their paper money could be exchanged for a fixed amount of gold or silver, which helped to reassure the public. That link has now been abandoned almost everywhere. Modern currencies are backed not by metal but by the confidence of the people who use them, which is perhaps the strongest evidence that trust, rather than any material, is what gives money its value.

stimuli.title: The Humble Pencil
stimuli.text:
In the sixteenth century, a large deposit of unusually pure graphite was found at Borrowdale, in the north of England. Local people at first used it to mark sheep, but it was soon cut into sticks for writing and drawing. Because pure graphite is soft and brittle, the sticks were wrapped in string or set into wooden holders. For a long time the deposit was so valuable that it was guarded, and supplies were controlled to keep prices high.

Other countries had no such source, and their pencils were often poor. In 1795, during a war that cut France off from English graphite, the French engineer Nicolas-Jacques Conté found a solution. He ground graphite into powder, mixed it with clay and baked the mixture. By changing the amount of clay, he could make leads that were harder or softer, so that one material could serve both artists and engineers.

The same basic method is still used today. Leads with more clay are harder and make paler lines, while those with more graphite are softer and darker. Ordinary pencils contain no lead at all; the name survives from an old belief that graphite was a form of the metal.

stimuli.title: Why Cities Stay Warm at Night
stimuli.text:
On a still summer evening, the centre of a large city can be several degrees warmer than the countryside around it. Scientists call this the urban heat island effect. Part of the cause lies in the materials cities are built from. Dark roads and roofs absorb sunlight during the day and release the heat slowly after dark, so city streets cool far less at night than open fields. Tall buildings make the problem worse by trapping warm air and blocking the breezes that might carry it away.

Human activity adds further heat. Cars, factories and air conditioners all release warmth into the streets, and in hot weather the extra air conditioning needed to keep buildings cool can itself raise outdoor temperatures. Cities also have fewer plants than the countryside. Trees and grass cool the air around them by releasing water vapour, and they shade the ground beneath them.

Many cities are now trying to reduce the effect. Some paint roofs white or pale colours so that they reflect more sunlight, while others plant trees along streets or cover roofs with plants. These measures matter because high night-time temperatures can be dangerous, especially for elderly people, who may be unable to recover from the heat of the day.
