questions.stem:
Mangroves cover a larger area in South Asia than in West Africa.

Does this agree with the information in the passage: True, False or Not Given?
questions.explanation: Paragraph A names both regions as places where mangroves grow but does not compare the area in each.

questions.stem:
Leaves and roots break down slowly in mangrove soil.

Does this agree with the information in the passage: True, False or Not Given?
questions.explanation: Paragraph D says dead leaves and roots decay very slowly because the soil is waterlogged and low in oxygen.

questions.stem:
Complete the summary. Choose ONE word from the list.

Some mangroves get rid of salt through special glands on their [[1]], which may glitter with crystals.
questions.explanation: Paragraph B says some species excrete salt through special glands on their leaves. Other species filter it at the roots instead.

questions.stem:
Complete the summary. Choose ONE word from the list.

In some species, arching [[1]] roots hold the trunk above the water like the legs of a stool.
questions.explanation: Paragraph B says arching prop roots support the trunk. The pencil-like roots stick out of the mud to take in air.

questions.stem:
Complete the sentence. Choose ONE word from the list.

Waves lose [[1]] as they pass between the trunks and roots of a mangrove forest.
questions.explanation: Paragraph C says waves lose energy as they pass between the trunks and roots, so their height falls.

questions.stem:
Answer the question. Choose ONE word from the list.

Which animals are farmed in the ponds that have replaced many mangrove forests? [[1]]
questions.explanation: Paragraph E says the forests have been cleared especially for ponds used to farm shrimp.

questions.stem:
Complete the sentence. Choose ONE word from the list.

Ecologists say the most successful restoration begins by restoring the flow of [[1]].
questions.explanation: Paragraph F says restoration should begin with restoring the flow of water, for example by breaking old pond walls, so seeds can settle naturally.

questions.stem:
The suggestion that museums may not need originals is based on a mistaken idea of their purpose.

Does this agree with the claims of the writer: Yes, No or Not Given?
questions.explanation: The writer says the question rests on a misunderstanding of what museums are for.

questions.stem:
Fogarty's argument about objects kept in storage is unreasonable.

Does this agree with the claims of the writer: Yes, No or Not Given?
questions.explanation: After setting out Fogarty's and Webb's points, the writer says both seem entirely reasonable.

questions.stem:
Visitors' feeling of connection with real objects is only a superstition.

Does this agree with the claims of the writer: Yes, No or Not Given?
questions.explanation: The writer raises the sceptics' view and answers only "Perhaps it is", then argues the feeling matters anyway. The writer neither agrees nor disagrees that it is a superstition.

questions.stem:
Museums should slow down digitisation until conservation budgets improve.

Does this agree with the claims of the writer: Yes, No or Not Given?
questions.explanation: The writer believes every museum should be scanning its collections as fast as funding allows.

questions.stem:
Most museum visitors prefer digital displays to written labels.

Does this agree with the claims of the writer: Yes, No or Not Given?
questions.explanation: Labels are never mentioned, and the writer gives no view on which visitors prefer.

questions.stem: What does the writer say about the case for the digital museum?
options: It ignores the needs of students
It is based on poor research
It deserves to be taken seriously
It is mainly about saving museums money
questions.explanation: The second paragraph opens: the case for the digital museum is not foolish, and it deserves a fair hearing. It is in fact partly about helping students.

questions.stem: According to Okafor, when is visitors' sense of connection strongest?
options: When the object is very old
When a guide explains the object
When they have seen a good copy first
When they know its makers handled it
questions.explanation: Okafor notes the feeling is strongest when visitors know the object was handled by the people who made and used it.

questions.stem: What is the writer's main point in the fifth paragraph?
options: A scan captures only part of an object
Scans are too expensive for most museums
Scans can show the chemistry of paint
Scanning can damage the surface of objects
questions.explanation: The fifth paragraph says every copy records only what its makers thought to record, so a scan misses paint chemistry, metal sources and future questions.

questions.stem: What does the writer see as the real threat to museums?
options: The spread of better and cheaper scanners
A lack of money for conservation
questions.explanation: The last paragraph says the real threat is not the scanner but the budget, because short funds tempt museums to let a digital record replace care of the object.

questions.stem: Which person argues that copies could allow objects to be returned to the countries they came from?
questions.explanation: The historian Marcus Webb says high-quality copies could allow originals to be returned while the museum still tells their story.

questions.stem: Which person has interviewed hundreds of museum visitors?
questions.explanation: The museum educator Ruth Okafor has interviewed hundreds of visitors about how they feel in front of real objects.

questions.stem:
Choose the correct ending for this sentence:

Fogarty argues that digitising objects kept in storage would ...
options: allow the originals to be sold
persuade museums to display more of them
help people who cannot visit them
reduce the cost of storing them
questions.explanation: Fogarty says digitising hidden objects would make them available to students and researchers who could never travel to see them.

questions.stem:
Choose the correct ending for this sentence:

Webb accepts that original objects should ...
options: be kept even if they are not displayed
always be returned to their countries of origin
be scanned before they are sold
questions.explanation: The fifth paragraph says Webb does not suggest originals should be destroyed, only that they need not always be on display.

questions.stem:
Complete the sentence. Choose ONE word from the list.

The writer believes that copies and originals are better understood as [[1]] than as competitors.
questions.explanation: The sixth paragraph says the mistake is to see copies and originals as competitors when they are better understood as partners.

questions.stem: Which heading best fits Paragraph B?
options: More than a new kind of box
The first container to cross an ocean
Resistance from dockworkers and their unions
questions.explanation: Paragraph B says McLean's insight was not the box itself but the system of ships, cranes, lorries and trains built around it. The Ideal X sailed along the coast from Newark to Houston, not across an ocean.

questions.stem: Which heading best fits Paragraph C?
options: More than a new kind of box
Faster ports and a changing waterfront
Risks of a highly connected system
questions.explanation: Paragraph C describes how boxes of different sizes did not fit other lines' ships, until international standards were agreed in the 1960s.

questions.stem: Which heading best fits Paragraph D?
options: Resistance from dockworkers and their unions
Faster ports and a changing waterfront
questions.explanation: Paragraph D covers quicker turnarounds, fewer dockworkers and old waterfront districts declining. Fewer jobs are mentioned, but not any resistance to the change.

questions.stem: Which heading best fits Paragraph E?
options: The first container to cross an ocean
Risks of a highly connected system
More than a new kind of box
Faster ports and a changing waterfront
questions.explanation: Paragraph E explains that cheap shipping let manufacturers build far from customers and assemble products from parts made in several countries.

questions.stem: Which heading best fits Paragraph F?
options: Resistance from dockworkers and their unions
Risks of a highly connected system
questions.explanation: Paragraph F names two weaknesses: a blockage at one large port delays goods worldwide, and few containers can be searched.

questions.stem:
McLean had worked in the trucking business.

Does this agree with the information in the passage: True, False or Not Given?
questions.explanation: Paragraph B calls McLean an American trucking businessman.

questions.stem:
The Ideal X was built specifically to carry containers.

Does this agree with the information in the passage: True, False or Not Given?
questions.explanation: Paragraph B says the Ideal X was a converted tanker, so it was not built for containers.

questions.stem:
The international container standards were first proposed by McLean.

Does this agree with the information in the passage: True, False or Not Given?
questions.explanation: Paragraph C says standards were agreed in the 1960s but does not say who proposed them.

questions.stem:
Complete the note. Choose ONE word from the list.

Ship capacity: measured in twenty-foot equivalent [[1]]
questions.explanation: Paragraph C says a ship's capacity is still described in twenty-foot equivalent units.

questions.stem:
Complete the sentence. Choose ONE word from the list.

Containers are lifted and locked together by their corner [[1]].
questions.explanation: Paragraph C mentions standards for the corner fittings by which containers are lifted and locked together.

questions.stem: According to Paragraph E, what do some economists believe about the container?
options: It raised the price of most goods
It mattered less than cheaper fuel
It expanded trade more than many agreements
It moved factories much closer to their customers
questions.explanation: Paragraph E says some economists argue the container did more to expand world trade than many trade agreements. Factories in fact moved further from customers.

questions.stem: Which problem with containers is mentioned in Paragraph F?
options: They rust quickly in salty air
They cannot be carried by train or lorry
Many of them are lost at sea
Few of them can be opened for checks
questions.explanation: Paragraph F says only a small proportion can be opened and searched, which makes customs checks harder. Trains are part of the system in Paragraph B.

questions.stem: Which heading best fits Paragraph B?
options: The role of parents on the first journey
How birds choose a winter home
Following the sun with an inner clock
Several cues that check each other
questions.explanation: Paragraph B describes starlings that followed the apparent position of the sun and explains that a sun compass also needs an internal body clock.

questions.stem: Which heading best fits Paragraph C?
options: Following the sun with an inner clock
The dangers of migrating at night
A sense of the Earth's magnetism
questions.explanation: Paragraph C reports that young birds in a planetarium learned which part of the sky the stars turn around. Night migration is mentioned, but its dangers are not.

questions.stem: Which heading best fits Paragraph D?
options: How birds choose a winter home
A sense of the Earth's magnetism
The dangers of migrating at night
questions.explanation: Paragraph D covers tests with artificial magnetic fields and two theories of how birds detect the field.

questions.stem: Which heading best fits Paragraph E?
options: A sense of the Earth's magnetism
Following the sun with an inner clock
The role of parents on the first journey
questions.explanation: Paragraph E describes shearwaters that could not find home when their sense of smell was blocked.

questions.stem: Which heading best fits Paragraph F?
options: How birds choose a winter home
The role of parents on the first journey
The dangers of migrating at night
Several cues that check each other
questions.explanation: Paragraph F says no single cue explains everything and that a system with several back-ups is more reliable. Experienced birds are compared with young ones, but parents are not discussed.

questions.stem: What did the starling experiments show?
options: The birds flew further when the sun was hidden
The birds changed direction to follow the sun
The birds ignored where the sun appeared
The birds could not migrate while caged
questions.explanation: Paragraph B says that when mirrors shifted the apparent position of the sun, the birds shifted their direction to match.

questions.stem: What did the planetarium study suggest about young birds?
options: They learn the pattern of the stars
They are born with a map of the stars
They prefer to migrate by day
questions.explanation: Paragraph C says the birds adjusted when the sky turned around a different star, suggesting they learn the pattern rather than being born with a fixed map.

questions.stem: What happened to shearwaters whose sense of smell was blocked?
options: They did better than the other group of birds
They struggled to find their way home
They were unable to fly normally
questions.explanation: Paragraph E says these birds flew normally but had great difficulty finding home. It was the birds with a disturbed magnetic sense that did much better.

questions.stem:
Complete the sentence. Choose ONE word from the list.

A bird that uses the sun as a compass must also keep track of the [[1]].
questions.explanation: Paragraph B says the sun moves across the sky, so a bird using it must also keep track of the time with an internal clock.

questions.stem:
Complete the summary. Choose ONE word from the list.

One theory says that chemical reactions in a bird's [[1]] may be affected by magnetism.
questions.explanation: Paragraph D says one theory points to chemical reactions in the eye. The beak belongs to the second theory, about iron-containing particles.

questions.stem: Which paragraph contains a reference to young birds travelling without adults?
questions.explanation: Paragraph A says many young birds make their first journey alone, without parents to follow.

questions.stem: Which paragraph contains a comparison between experienced birds and first-year birds?
questions.explanation: Paragraph F says experienced travellers blown off course are often better at returning to their route than first-year birds.

questions.stem: Which heading best fits Paragraph B?
options: Why some people avoid eating wheat bread
How the dough gets its stretch
Gas that makes the dough rise
The real reason bread goes stale
questions.explanation: Paragraph B explains how two groups of wheat proteins link into stretchy gluten chains that make dough elastic.

questions.stem: Which heading best fits Paragraph C?
options: The best way to store flour
Wild yeasts and a long-lived starter
How the dough gets its stretch
Gas that makes the dough rise
questions.explanation: Paragraph C describes yeast releasing carbon dioxide that the gluten traps in bubbles, so the dough swells. Wild yeasts belong to sourdough in Paragraph D.

questions.stem: Which heading best fits Paragraph D?
options: Gas that makes the dough rise
Why some people avoid eating wheat bread
Changes in the heat of the oven
Wild yeasts and a long-lived starter
questions.explanation: Paragraph D is about sourdough: wild yeasts and bacteria in a starter that some bakeries have kept for decades.

questions.stem: Which heading best fits Paragraph E?
options: Changes in the heat of the oven
The real reason bread goes stale
How the dough gets its stretch
The best way to store flour
questions.explanation: Paragraph E describes what happens during baking: a final rise, proteins setting and the crust forming. It does not discuss choosing an oven.

questions.stem: Which heading best fits Paragraph F?
options: The best way to store flour
The real reason bread goes stale
Wild yeasts and a long-lived starter
Changes in the heat of the oven
Why some people avoid eating wheat bread
questions.explanation: Paragraph F says staling is caused mainly by a change in the starch, not by drying out. Storage is about bread, not flour.

questions.stem:
Early bakers understood why dough rose.

Does this agree with the information in the passage: True, False or Not Given?
questions.explanation: Paragraph A says bakers knew that dough would rise but had no idea why.

questions.stem:
Yeast produces some alcohol as it feeds.

Does this agree with the information in the passage: True, False or Not Given?
questions.explanation: Paragraph C says yeast releases carbon dioxide gas and small amounts of alcohol.

questions.stem:
Sourdough bread contains more protein than ordinary bread.

Does this agree with the information in the passage: True, False or Not Given?
questions.explanation: Paragraph D compares sourdough's taste and freshness but says nothing about its protein content.

questions.stem: Which paragraph contains an explanation of why some flours give flat results?
questions.explanation: Paragraph B says flours with little of the gluten proteins, such as rice or maize, give flat or crumbly results on their own.

questions.stem: Which paragraph contains a reason not to keep bread in a refrigerator?
questions.explanation: Paragraph F says staling is fastest just above freezing, so bread in a refrigerator usually goes stale sooner than bread at room temperature.

questions.stem:
Choose the correct ending for this sentence:

Dough that rises very quickly may ...
questions.explanation: Paragraph C says warmth speeds up rising, but dough that rises too quickly may develop less flavour. Staying fresh for longer is due to the acids in sourdough.

questions.stem:
Choose the correct ending for this sentence:

The brown colour of the crust comes from ...
questions.explanation: Paragraph E says sugars and proteins react together on the hot surface to form the brown crust. Starch crystals belong to staling in Paragraph F.

questions.stem:
The five-day week has always been the normal pattern of work.

Does this agree with the claims of the writer: Yes, No or Not Given?
questions.explanation: The writer calls the five-day week a relatively recent invention with nothing fixed about it.

questions.stem:
The findings about workers' well-being can be trusted.

Does this agree with the claims of the writer: Yes, No or Not Given?
questions.explanation: The writer says the well-being findings are consistent across very different workplaces and sees little reason to doubt them.

questions.stem:
The four-day week is a bad idea and should be abandoned.

Does this agree with the claims of the writer: Yes, No or Not Given?
questions.explanation: The last paragraph begins: none of this persuades me that the idea should be dropped.

questions.stem:
Governments should make the four-day week a legal requirement.

Does this agree with the claims of the writer: Yes, No or Not Given?
questions.explanation: The writer asks for patience and careful measurement but never mentions laws or governments.

questions.stem:
A four-day week is easier to organise in an office than in a hospital.

Does this agree with the claims of the writer: Yes, No or Not Given?
questions.explanation: The writer says a shorter week is easier to arrange in an office, where work can be rescheduled, than in a hospital, care home or factory.

questions.stem: What does Henning report about staff after the change?
options: Longer hours on the remaining working days
Less stress and fewer sick days
questions.explanation: Henning reports large falls in stress and in days taken off sick. Productivity is discussed separately and is not her finding.

questions.stem: Why does Pryce doubt some of the productivity findings?
options: The trials measured stress, not output
Most trials took place in factories
The firms chose to join the trials
Workers were paid less during the trials
questions.explanation: Pryce warns that the organisations chose to take part, so they may already have been well suited to the change, and that many trials were short.

questions.stem: What does the writer compare the four-day week with in the last paragraph?
options: The earlier move to a five-day week
The spread of working from home offices
questions.explanation: The writer says the five-day week was once a radical demand adopted gradually, industry by industry, and that something similar may happen now.

questions.stem:
Complete the summary. Choose ONE word from the list.

Employees said the extra day gave them time for exercise, family and the [[1]] that used to crowd their weekends.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says the extra day gave time for exercise, family and the errands that otherwise crowded their weekends.

questions.stem:
Complete the sentence. Choose ONE word from the list.

In a hospital, a four-day week for each worker usually means hiring more [[1]].
questions.explanation: Pryce points out that in settings that run continuously, a four-day week usually means hiring more staff, which raises costs.

questions.stem: Which person warns that the trials may have involved firms already suited to the change?
questions.explanation: The economist Owen Pryce warns that the organisations chose to take part and may already have been well suited to the change.

questions.stem: Which person suggests that some workers might prefer more paid hours?
questions.explanation: The union researcher Amira Saleh adds that workers on low pay may prefer extra paid hours to an extra day off.

questions.stem:
The story of the lone genius is accurate in most cases.

Does this agree with the claims of the writer: Yes, No or Not Given?
questions.explanation: The writer says the story is, in most cases, misleading.

questions.stem:
Brandt's evidence is hard to reject.

Does this agree with the claims of the writer: Yes, No or Not Given?
questions.explanation: After describing Brandt's cases, the writer says: I find his evidence difficult to dismiss.

questions.stem:
Junior staff in famous laboratories were usually well paid.

Does this agree with the claims of the writer: Yes, No or Not Given?
questions.explanation: The writer says junior staff were rarely named and sometimes lost credit, but says nothing about their pay.

questions.stem:
Individual talent plays no part in discovery.

Does this agree with the claims of the writer: Yes, No or Not Given?
questions.explanation: The writer says none of this means individuals do not matter, since some people clearly have unusual talent, energy or imagination.

questions.stem:
Persistence matters more than a mysterious gift.

Does this agree with the claims of the writer: Yes, No or Not Given?
questions.explanation: The writer finds Adair's message encouraging because it suggests persistence counts for more than a mysterious gift.

questions.stem: Which person found that credit for an idea sometimes went to someone who did not have it first?
questions.explanation: Varela studied laboratory notebooks and found credit was often given to the person in charge for ideas first noted by junior staff.

questions.stem: Which person collected cases of the same discovery made independently?
questions.explanation: The historian Felix Brandt collected hundreds of cases in which two or more people made the same discovery independently.

questions.stem: Which person found that outstanding creators produce a great deal of ordinary work?
questions.explanation: The psychologist Tom Adair showed that outstanding creators produce a large amount of work, much of it unremarkable.

questions.stem:
Choose the correct ending for this sentence:

According to Brandt, new ideas tend to appear when ...
options: a single inventor works in isolation
rival laboratories share their notes openly
the knowledge they need is widely shared
questions.explanation: Brandt argues ideas appear when the knowledge and tools needed for them have become widely available, so another inventor would soon have made the same breakthrough.

questions.stem:
Choose the correct ending for this sentence:

The writer fears that the myth may ...
options: put young people off creative work
make research teams work much harder
questions.explanation: The last paragraph says the myth may discourage young people who do not see themselves as geniuses from attempting creative work.

questions.stem:
Complete the summary. Choose ONE word from the list.

Famous laboratories were busy workplaces where teams of [[1]] built equipment, ran tests and recorded results.
questions.explanation: The third paragraph says teams of assistants built equipment, ran tests and recorded results.

questions.stem:
Complete the sentence. Choose ONE word from the list.

Varela studied the [[1]] kept in laboratories to see where ideas first appeared.
questions.explanation: The third paragraph says Varela studied the notebooks kept in such workplaces.

questions.stem:
The belief that adults cannot learn languages well has no basis at all.

Does this agree with the claims of the writer: Yes, No or Not Given?
questions.explanation: The writer says the belief contains some truth, about pronunciation, though it has been stretched too far.

questions.stem:
The evidence about pronunciation and age is convincing.

Does this agree with the claims of the writer: Yes, No or Not Given?
questions.explanation: The writer says that on pronunciation the evidence is strong, and accepts it.

questions.stem:
Evening classes are the most effective way for adults to learn a language.

Does this agree with the claims of the writer: Yes, No or Not Given?
questions.explanation: Evening classes appear only in Karim's comparison; the writer never says which way of learning works best.

questions.stem:
Age has no effect at all on how a person learns a language.

Does this agree with the claims of the writer: Yes, No or Not Given?
questions.explanation: The writer says: I do not want to pretend that age makes no difference.

questions.stem:
Most adults can learn to communicate with confidence in a new language.

Does this agree with the claims of the writer: Yes, No or Not Given?
questions.explanation: The writer says confident, accurate communication is well within reach of most adults who are willing to put in the time.

questions.stem:
Schools should start teaching foreign languages at a younger age.

Does this agree with the claims of the writer: Yes, No or Not Given?
questions.explanation: The writer discusses children and adults as learners but gives no view on when schools should start teaching languages.

questions.stem: What does Karim argue about comparing children with adult learners?
options: It reflects opportunity more than age
It is unfair to adult learners' memory
It should include tests of accent
It shows that age is the main factor
questions.explanation: Karim argues that comparing an immersed child with an adult in an evening class tells us more about opportunity than about age.

questions.stem: According to Tanaka, which adults are more likely to keep studying?
options: Those who began before their teens
Those who aim simply to become fluent
questions.explanation: Tanaka found adults with specific practical goals, such as following a news broadcast, are more likely to keep studying than those aiming simply at fluency.

questions.stem:
Lindqvist has tested several thousand language learners.

Does this agree with the information in the passage: True, False or Not Given?
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says Lindqvist has tested several thousand learners.

questions.stem:
Lindqvist found that no late starter ever reached a native-like accent.

Does this agree with the information in the passage: True, False or Not Given?
questions.explanation: Lindqvist found a native-like accent is rare among late starters, though not impossible, which contradicts the statement.

questions.stem:
Choose the correct ending for this sentence:

In the early stages of learning, adults often ...
options: lose interest more quickly than children
questions.explanation: The third paragraph says adults often make faster early progress because they understand explanations, use memory strategies and draw on their first language.

questions.stem:
Choose the correct ending for this sentence:

Children usually overtake adults only after ...
options: a few hours of study each week
many years of living in the language
they have reached their early teens
they have learned all the grammar rules
questions.explanation: The third paragraph says children catch up and overtake adults only after many years of living immersed in the language.

questions.stem: Which paragraph contains a description of the sounds made on a healthy reef?
questions.explanation: Paragraph A describes the snapping of shrimp, the grunts and pops of fish and the scraping of animals feeding on coral.

questions.stem: Which paragraph contains an account of an experiment with loudspeakers in open water?
questions.explanation: Paragraph B describes recordings played through loudspeakers in open water that attracted fish larvae. The loudspeakers in Paragraph D were on patches of dead coral.

questions.stem: Which paragraph contains a suggestion that recordings could be used to check the health of reefs?
questions.explanation: Paragraph C says some scientists suggest sound recordings could monitor reef health cheaply.

questions.stem: Which paragraph contains a warning that attracting fish does not mean a reef has been restored?
questions.explanation: Paragraph E says attracting fish is not the same as restoring a reef, because corals will not recover in water that stays too warm or polluted.

questions.stem: Which paragraph contains a reference to noise made by ships?
questions.explanation: Paragraph F says the engines of ships and boats are loud underwater and can interfere with fish hearing.

questions.stem:
Reef noise was once mainly treated as something to remove from recordings.

Does this agree with the information in the passage: True, False or Not Given?
questions.explanation: Paragraph A says the noise was treated as background, something to be filtered out of recordings.

questions.stem:
Sound travels further than light underwater.

Does this agree with the information in the passage: True, False or Not Given?
questions.explanation: Paragraph B says sound travels well underwater, much further than light.

questions.stem:
The loudspeaker study on the damaged reef lasted two years.

Does this agree with the information in the passage: True, False or Not Given?
questions.explanation: Paragraph D says the results came over several weeks, which contradicts a two-year study.

questions.stem:
Complete the note. Choose ONE word from the list.

Monitoring reefs with sound: a microphone on the sea floor can record for weeks without a [[1]].
questions.explanation: Paragraph C says a microphone left on the sea floor can record for weeks without a diver.

questions.stem:
Complete the sentence. Choose ONE word from the list.

The scientists suggest combining sound with other methods, such as replanting coral [[1]].
questions.explanation: Paragraph E names replanting coral fragments as another tool. Patches of dead coral were part of the experiment in Paragraph D.

questions.stem: What happened on the coral patches that had loudspeakers?
options: The dead coral began to grow again
More fish and more species arrived
The water around them became cooler
questions.explanation: Paragraph D says these patches attracted considerably more young fish and a wider range of species than silent patches. Paragraph E says the corals will not recover from sound alone.

questions.stem: What is the main point of Paragraph F?
options: Human noise may hide the sound of reefs
Ships cause most of the damage to corals
Reefs are louder near busy coasts
Fish have learned to avoid boats
questions.explanation: Paragraph F says engine noise can drown out a healthy reef's sounds and interfere with fish hearing, so the soundscape itself needs protecting.

questions.stem: Which person created a way of describing the strength of the wind?
questions.explanation: In 1805 Beaufort devised a scale for describing wind strength, at first by its effect on a warship's sails.

questions.stem: Which person began publishing forecasts in a national newspaper?
questions.explanation: FitzRoy began publishing what he called forecasts in a national newspaper in 1861.

questions.stem: Which person led a group that developed the idea of fronts?
questions.explanation: The Bergen group led by Vilhelm Bjerknes developed the idea that boundaries between bodies of air, called fronts, bring changeable weather.

questions.stem: Which person imagined thousands of people calculating the weather together?
questions.explanation: Richardson imagined a vast hall in which thousands of people would perform calculations fast enough to keep ahead of the weather.

questions.stem: Which person set up a network of coastal stations that sent reports to London?
questions.explanation: FitzRoy set up coastal stations that telegraphed observations to London and issued storm warnings from them.

questions.stem:
Complete the sentence. Choose ONE word from the list.

Beaufort's scale at first described the wind by its effect on the [[1]] of a warship.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says the scale described the wind at first by its effect on the sails of a warship.

questions.stem:
Complete the summary. Choose ONE word from the list.

The Bergen scientists called the boundaries between bodies of air with different temperatures [[1]].
questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph says the boundaries between bodies of air were called fronts, a word taken partly from the battlefronts of the war.

questions.stem:
Answer the question. Choose ONE word from the list.

About how long did Richardson spend on his calculation? Six [[1]]
questions.explanation: The fifth paragraph says he spent around six weeks calculating. Six hours was the period his forecast covered.

questions.stem: Why was the telegraph so important to weather forecasting?
options: Reports could be sent in minutes
questions.explanation: The third paragraph says the telegraph changed everything because weather reports could be sent across a country in minutes, faster than the weather itself.

questions.stem: What does the writer say about Richardson's forecast?
options: It was made with an early electronic computer
It was wrong, but his method was sound
It was accurate but took far too long
questions.explanation: The fifth paragraph says his result was badly wrong, partly because of errors in the starting data, but his method was sound.

questions.stem:
FitzRoy's storm warnings were valued by many sailors.

Does this agree with the information in the passage: True, False or Not Given?
questions.explanation: The third paragraph says the storm warnings were valued by many sailors, even though his forecasts were often wrong.

questions.stem:
Richardson worked with Bjerknes in Bergen.

Does this agree with the information in the passage: True, False or Not Given?
questions.explanation: The passage says Bjerknes believed weather could be calculated and that Richardson attempted it, but never says where Richardson worked or that they worked together.

questions.stem:
Desalination is a recent invention.

Does this agree with the information in the passage: True, False or Not Given?
questions.explanation: Paragraph A says the process is far from new, and Paragraph B says sailors used simple distillation centuries ago.

questions.stem:
Reverse osmosis membranes must be replaced every year.

Does this agree with the information in the passage: True, False or Not Given?
questions.explanation: Paragraph D says the membranes are delicate and easily blocked, but nothing is said about how often they are replaced.

questions.stem:
Minerals are added to desalinated water partly to protect pipes.

Does this agree with the information in the passage: True, False or Not Given?
questions.explanation: Paragraph D says minerals are added back both for taste and to protect pipes from corrosion.

questions.stem:
Brine is lighter than seawater.

Does this agree with the information in the passage: True, False or Not Given?
questions.explanation: Paragraph E says brine is heavier than seawater, so it can sink and spread along the seabed.

questions.stem:
Label the diagram. Choose ONE word from the list.

A diagram of a reverse osmosis unit, described in words: seawater enters on the left under high pressure; in the middle is a thin [[1]] with tiny pores; fresh water collects on the right; the concentrated salty liquid left behind, called brine, flows out on the left.
questions.explanation: Paragraph C says seawater is pushed against a membrane, a thin sheet with pores so small that water passes through but most salts do not. Reverse osmosis needs no heating.

questions.stem:
Label the diagram. Choose ONE word from the list.

A diagram of a reverse osmosis unit, described in words: seawater enters on the left under high pressure; in the middle is a thin membrane with tiny pores; fresh water collects on the right; the concentrated salty liquid left behind, called [[1]], flows out on the left.
questions.explanation: Paragraph C says the concentrated salty liquid left on the other side of the membrane is known as brine. Vapour belongs to distillation.

questions.stem:
Answer the question. Choose ONE word from the list.

What do the filters remove before seawater reaches the membranes? Sand, seaweed and tiny [[1]]
questions.explanation: Paragraph D says the filters remove sand, seaweed and tiny organisms. Salts are removed by the membrane itself.

questions.stem:
Complete the sentence. Choose ONE word from the list.

Engineers design outlets that release brine through many small [[1]] so that it mixes quickly.
questions.explanation: Paragraph E says outlets spread the brine through many small openings so it mixes quickly with the surrounding water.

questions.stem: Why does reverse osmosis usually use less energy than distillation?
options: It does not need the water to be heated
It treats smaller volumes of water
It produces no brine at all
Its pumps run for only part of every day
questions.explanation: Paragraph C says no heating is needed, although the pumps still need a large and steady supply of electricity. It does produce brine.

questions.stem: What do some researchers hope to do with brine?
options: Use it to clean the blocked membranes
questions.explanation: Paragraph E says some researchers are exploring ways to extract useful materials from brine, turning a waste product into a resource.

questions.stem: Which paragraph contains a reason why the water from a plant is not left completely pure?
questions.explanation: Paragraph D says the treated water lacks minerals, so small amounts are added back for taste and to protect pipes.

questions.stem: Which paragraph contains a reference to desalination being used on ships long ago?
questions.explanation: Paragraph B says sailors used simple versions of distillation on board ship centuries ago.

questions.stem:
Early coins were trusted because of the metal they contained.

Does this agree with the information in the passage: True, False or Not Given?
questions.explanation: Paragraph A says a coin was trusted because the metal it contained had value, whoever had made it.

questions.stem:
The Chinese government created the receipts before merchants began to use them.

Does this agree with the information in the passage: True, False or Not Given?
questions.explanation: Paragraph B says traders began using receipts first, and the government took over their issue later, in the early eleventh century.

questions.stem:
Marco Polo brought paper notes back with him to Europe.

Does this agree with the information in the passage: True, False or Not Given?
questions.explanation: Paragraph D says Marco Polo described the notes, but not whether he brought any home.

questions.stem:
Choose the correct ending for this sentence:

Traders in Sichuan left their coins with dealers because ...
options: the coins were heavy to carry
questions.explanation: Paragraph B says the iron coins were so awkward to carry in large amounts that traders left them with dealers for written receipts.

questions.stem:
Choose the correct ending for this sentence:

When rulers printed more notes, ...
options: people trusted the notes even more
each note lost some of its value
questions.explanation: Paragraph C says that when rulers printed more notes, the value of each note fell and prices rose.

questions.stem:
Choose the correct ending for this sentence:

Many of Marco Polo's readers in Europe ...
options: began printing their own paper notes
asked for notes made of bark
travelled to China to see it
found his account hard to believe
questions.explanation: Paragraph D ends: many of his readers in Europe found the account hard to believe.

questions.stem:
Complete the summary. Choose ONE word from the list.

The notes Marco Polo described were made from the bark of [[1]] trees.
questions.explanation: Paragraph D says the paper was made from the bark of mulberry trees.

questions.stem:
Complete the sentence. Choose ONE word from the list.

The bank in Stockholm failed after it issued too many [[1]].
questions.explanation: Paragraph E says too many notes were issued and the bank failed within a few years.

questions.stem:
Complete the note. Choose ONE word from the list.

Modern currencies: backed by the [[1]] of the people who use them, not by metal
questions.explanation: Paragraph F says modern currencies are backed not by metal but by the confidence of the people who use them.

questions.stem: What is the writer's main point in Paragraph F?
options: Trust is what gives money its value
Gold is the safest form of money
Paper money should be linked to metal
questions.explanation: Paragraph F concludes that trust, rather than any material, is what gives money its value. The link to gold has been abandoned, and the writer does not call for it back.

questions.stem: Which paragraph contains an account of how one European experiment with banknotes failed?
questions.explanation: Paragraph E says the Stockholm bank issued too many notes and failed within a few years.

questions.stem: Which paragraph contains the disadvantages as well as the advantages of paper money?
questions.explanation: Paragraph C lists the advantages (light, easy to transport, cheap) and the new risk of falling value when rulers print more notes.

questions.stem:
People first used the Borrowdale graphite to mark sheep.

Does this agree with the information in the passage: True, False or Not Given?
questions.explanation: The first paragraph says local people at first used it to mark sheep.

questions.stem:
Anyone was free to take graphite from the Borrowdale deposit.

Does this agree with the information in the passage: True, False or Not Given?
questions.explanation: The first paragraph says the deposit was guarded and supplies were controlled, which contradicts the statement.

questions.stem:
Conté's pencils were cheaper than English pencils.

Does this agree with the information in the passage: True, False or Not Given?
questions.explanation: The passage explains how Conté made his leads but never compares their price with English pencils.

questions.stem: What did changing the amount of clay allow Conté to do?
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says that by changing the amount of clay he could make leads that were harder or softer, for artists and engineers alike.

questions.stem: Which kind of lead makes the palest line?
options: One that was baked for longer
questions.explanation: The last paragraph says leads with more clay are harder and make paler lines, while more graphite gives softer, darker lines.

questions.stem:
Complete the sentence. Choose ONE word from the list.

Despite their name, ordinary pencils contain no [[1]].
questions.explanation: The last paragraph says ordinary pencils contain no lead at all; the name comes from an old belief that graphite was a form of the metal.

questions.stem:
City streets cool down more at night than open fields.

Does this agree with the information in the passage: True, False or Not Given?
questions.explanation: The first paragraph says city streets cool far less at night than open fields.

questions.stem:
Air conditioning can raise temperatures outside buildings.

Does this agree with the information in the passage: True, False or Not Given?
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says the extra air conditioning needed in hot weather can itself raise outdoor temperatures.

questions.stem:
The heat island effect is strongest in winter.

Does this agree with the information in the passage: True, False or Not Given?
questions.explanation: The passage describes a summer evening but never compares the strength of the effect in different seasons.

questions.stem: How do tall buildings add to the heat island effect?
options: They absorb more sunlight than roads
They cast too little shade on streets
They trap warm air and block breezes
questions.explanation: The first paragraph says tall buildings make the problem worse by trapping warm air and blocking the breezes that might carry it away.

questions.stem: Why does the writer mention elderly people?
options: Hot nights can be dangerous for them
They use the most air conditioning
They mostly live in city centres
They prefer roofs painted pale colours
questions.explanation: The last paragraph says high night-time temperatures can be dangerous, especially for elderly people who may not recover from the heat of the day.

questions.stem:
Complete the summary. Choose ONE word from the list.

Trees and grass cool the air around them by releasing water [[1]].
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says trees and grass cool the air by releasing water vapour and by shading the ground.
